paper_title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robot foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, motivating low-cost offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To test this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to robotics and make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a low-cost, representation-level view of robot foundation models that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal.

Figure 1 Left: We test the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) in robotics, using imagetext features as the sensory representation and end-effector trajectories as the motor representation: more capable embodied model should have sensory representations that align more closely with this motor representation. To validate this, we define Sensorimotor Alignment (S2). Introduction Robot foundation models increasingly build on large pretrained vision-language models [3, 4], video models [50], and world action models [5, 15, 28]. Yet selecting and evaluating these models remains expensive: the most reliable test is still closed-loop rollout in simulation [30, 33] or the real world [1, 9], where evaluation is slow, noisy, and benchmark-dependent. This expense motivates low-cost offline proxies for policy capability. natural approach is to use existing perception-side proxies, such as visual question answering scores for VLMs [31, 57] or pixel-level video quality for world models [18, 23, 52]. However, these metrics measure passive perception or generation quality, not whether representation is organized for action [24, 35, 47, 59]. Two scenes may look visually different but require similar robot motions; conversely, two visually similar scenes may demand different trajectories. For robot task success, model must produce different motions across tasks even in similar scenes. This requires aligning the sensory representation with the motor representation. This perspective connects robotics to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) [21], which argues that as models of different modalities scale and solve diverse tasks, they are converging to shared statistical model of reality in each of their own representation spaces. For example, images and text are two projections of the same underlying world. As vision and language models scale, they increasingly agree on the relative distances between data points. We bring PRH to robotics and ask: can physical robot motion be viewed as another projection of that same world, such that more capable embodied models better align their vision and language representations with the structure of motion trajectories? We test this prediction of PRH: the more capable an embodied model is, the more closely its sensory representations align with its motor representation. In other words, episodes nearby in sensory representation space should also be nearby in motor representation space. We formalize this as Sensorimotor Alignment (S2), training-free metric, illustrated in Figure 1. For each episode in robot dataset, models image and text features form its sensory representation, and the recorded end-effector trajectory forms its motor representation. We measure alignment by comparing each episodes nearest neighbors in sensory and motor spaces. More overlap between the two neighbor sets means stronger sensorimotor alignment. In Section 3, we show that S2 correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, in simulated and real-world settings. The correlation is strong for VisionLanguage-Action models (VLAs) in closed-loop manipulation, indicating that models with higher sensorimotor alignment tend to perform better. S2 computed on raw Vision-Language Models (VLMs) also correlates with the task success of the resulting VLAs, more strongly than their visual question answering (VQA) scores do. For World Action Models (WAMs), S2 likewise correlates more strongly with task success than video-quality metrics such as FID [18], SSIM [52], and PSNR [19], and for real-robot policies, S2 computed offline correlates with physical-robot task success on shared set of tasks. Across these settings, sensorimotor alignment correlates with task success more closely than VQA or video-quality metrics. Prior work has observed several phenomena in VLAs and WAMs only through closedloop results, without explaining them at the representation level. We use S2 to supply that explanation, as shown in Section 4. For example, fine-tuned VLAs often ignore the language instruction and act mainly on what they see; we find that their task success correlates with the S2 of their vision features, not their text features. Our contributions are threefold: Inspired by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, we propose new view of embodiment: more capable embodied models should align their sensory representations more closely with the structure of motion trajectories. To test this, we introduce S2, training-free offline metric that measures alignment between sensory and motor representations. Across model families, in simulation and on real robots, S2 correlates positively with task success, making it low-cost offline proxy for choosing models before closed-loop evaluation. Furthermore, we use S2 to explain, at the representation level, several phenomena in VLAs and WAMs that were previously observed only through closed-loop results, making it diagnostic tool for understanding how design choices shape embodied models. We make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering low-cost, representation-level view of robot foundation models that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal. 2. Measuring Sensorimotor Alignment Motivated by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) [21], we hypothesize that the more capable an embodied model is, the more closely its sensory representations align with its motor representation. Here, sensory representations are the models image and text features, and each episodes end-effector trajectory is its motor representation. To make this alignment measurable, we define Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) by constructing both representations and comparing their neighborhoods, as follows: Reference dataset. To measure cross-modal alignment, we use the DROID [26] and BridgeDataV2 [49] datasets, which pair sensory inputs with physical motions. From dataset, we sample 𝑁 episodes and compute both representations from each episode. For episode 𝑖, we randomly sample one image frame and pair it with the task instruction; this imagetext pair forms the sensory input x𝑖. Sampling details are provided in Appendix A.1. Sensory representation. For each episode 𝑖, we encode the image frame and text instruction with the vision and text encoders of robot foundation model, obtaining sensory embedding z𝑖 = 𝑓 (x𝑖) R𝑑 , where 𝑓 applies the vision encoder to the image and the text encoder to the instruction, and we average-pool the output token features into single 𝑑-dimensional vector. 3 Figure 2 Measuring Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) by nearest-neighbor overlap. For the query episode (left), sensory neighbors (bottom right) have similar vision-text features, and motor neighbors (top right) have similar trajectories. Green checks mark shared neighbors; red crosses mark neighbors found only in the sensory set. larger overlap means that episodes with similar sensory representations also follow similar motor trajectories. Motor representation. For the sampled frame in x𝑖, we extract end-effector positions, orientations, and gripper states over the next ℎ steps, forming episode 𝑖s motor representation: 𝝉𝑖 = (𝑥𝑖, 𝑦𝑖, 𝑧𝑖, 𝜙𝑖, 𝜃𝑖, 𝜓𝑖, 𝑔𝑖) Rℎ7, where row 𝑢 is the state 𝑢 steps after the sampled frame: 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧 are position coordinates, 𝜙, 𝜃, 𝜓 are roll, pitch, and yaw angles, and 𝑔 is the recorded gripper coordinate. We encode positions as vectors in R3 and orientation angles as rotations in SO(3) so that distances reflect the geometry of translations and rotations. Details are in Appendix A.2. Sensorimotor alignment. We measure alignment with mutual nearest-neighbor metric comparing the 𝑘-nearest-neighbor sets in sensory and motor spaces; greater overlap indicates stronger alignment between an episodes sensory and motor representations. We use cosine distance in sensory space and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) [37, 41] in motor space to compare trajectories at different speeds. For episodes 𝑖 and 𝑗: 𝑑sensory(𝑖, 𝑗) = 1 cos(z𝑖, 𝑗), 𝑑motor(𝑖, 𝑗) = DTW(𝝉𝑖, 𝝉 𝑗). Smaller distances mean closer neighbors. Appendices A.2A.3 detail DTW and normalization. For each episode 𝑖, we use 𝑑sensory to form the sensory 𝑘-nearest-neighbor set Nsensory(𝑖) and 𝑑motor to form the motor 𝑘-nearest-neighbor set Nmotor(𝑖). In practice, our reported S2 uses centered, normalized variant of CKNNA with 𝑘 = 10 neighbors unless stated otherwise; details are given in Appendix A.3. 3. Sensorimotor Alignment Correlates with Robot Task Success Rate The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) [21] argues that as models of different modalities become more capable, their representations converge toward shared statistical model of reality. 4 While the evidence for PRH comes from observational data such as images and text, robotics adds the motion the robot executes, which an embodied model must produce rather than observe. We test the prediction that models whose imagetext representations align more closely with end-effector trajectories should achieve higher downstream task success. We quantify this alignment using Sensorimotor Alignment (S2), which compares episode neighborhoods in sensory and motor space, as defined in Section 2. positive correlation between S2 and task success would provide empirical support for this PRH-inspired view of embodiment. It would also support using S2 as low-cost offline proxy for deciding which models to evaluate in closed loop first. Section 3.1 establishes this positive correlation across 3 model families and real-robot policies. Section 3.2 shows that S2 correlates with task success more closely than VQA and video-quality metrics. Section 3.3 shows that the correlation holds across computation settings and drops in negative control with mismatched embodiment. 3.1. S2 Correlates with Task Success Across Model Families In Figure 3, we test 3 model families and real-robot policies, comparing each models S2 on reference dataset (𝑥-axis) with its downstream manipulation success rate (𝑦-axis). (a) (b) (c) (d) Figure 3 Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) correlates with task success across model families and in simulated and real-world evaluations. Each panel plots offline S2 (𝑥-axis) against downstream task success rate (𝑦-axis) for (a) fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs), (b) raw vision-language models (VLMs), (c) world action models (WAMs), and (d) real-robot policies. For raw VLMs, task success is measured after VLA fine-tuning. These correlations (Pearsons 𝑟; unadjusted one-tailed 𝑝-values) support S2 as an offline proxy across model families. Vision-language-action models (VLAs). We test 12 VLAs against their SimplerEnv [30] success rates. In Figure 3a, the Pearson correlation 𝑟 =+0.717 is strong, with model-bootstrap 95% confidence interval of [+0.436, +0.912]. Thus, models with higher sensorimotor alignment tend to achieve higher task success rates. The correlation holds across reference datasets, model families, scales, and VLA training setups, as shown in Figure 6 and Appendix B.2. Vision-language models (VLMs). We ask whether S2 computed on raw VLM, before any robot fine-tuning, correlates with the task success of the VLA that is later fine-tuned from that backbone. We compute S2 for 8 raw VLM backbones from VLM4VLA [59] and compare it with the SimplerEnv [30] success rates of the resulting VLAs. We find strong correlation, 𝑟 = +0.681 with one-tailed 𝑝 = 0.031, as shown in Figure 3b. S2 can therefore identify promising VLM backbones before costly VLA fine-tuning. Appendix B.3 lists the backbones and S2 settings. World action models (WAMs). We also test WAMs, which build on video generators rather than VLMs. We compute S2 for 6 WAMs on the bimanual ALOHA dataset [61] and compare it with their success rates on RoboTwin 2.0 [33]. For WAMs, the sensory representation is the video-generator latent used for action decoding, and all 6 models share the same ALOHA trajectories and S2 settings. S2 again correlates strongly, 𝑟 = +0.718 with one-tailed 𝑝 = 0.054, as shown in Figure 3c. Appendix B.4 lists the 6 WAMs and shared evaluation protocol. 5 Real-robot policies. We test whether the correlation observed in simulation extends to real robots. Because real-world success rates depend on many factors, such as the task set, robot, cameras, and protocol, we take them all from one shared evaluation: the physical-robot results that MolmoB0T [11] reports for 5 policies on 40 tasks. We then compute S2 for their public checkpoints on the same DROID reference dataset. We find strong correlation with real-robot success, 𝑟 = +0.831 with one-tailed 𝑝 = 0.041, as shown in Figure 3d. Appendix B.5 describes the shared evaluation conditions and checkpoint scoring. We further validate that S2 correlates with downstream task success for frozen vision backbones under low-data behavior cloning and visual-reward learning, as shown in Appendix B.6. 3.2. S2 Correlates with Task Success More Closely Than Alternative Metrics Prior work asks whether offline scores correlate with downstream task performance. VLM4VLA [59] examines the correlation between VQA benchmark scores and the performance of the resulting VLA policies, finding weak or even negative correlations. For video models, Tian et al. [47] find that the quality of predicted video agrees inconsistently with downstream performance across tasks. common limitation is that these metrics measure language understanding or pixel-level video quality, neither of which depends on the motion the robot must execute. S2 instead compares the nearest-neighbor sets of sensory embeddings and motor trajectories. As we show below, S2 correlates more strongly with task success rate than any VQA or video-quality metric we evaluate. S2 correlates with VLA success rate where VQA scores do not. We compare S2 with aggregate VQA scores as offline proxies, using the same 8 raw VLM backbones and evaluation setting as in Section 3.1. We find that VQA scores show virtually no correlation with VLA success rate, at 𝑟 = 0.154 (right panel of Figure 4). S2, by contrast, correlates strongly, at 𝑟 = +0.681 with one-tailed 𝑝 = 0.031 (left panel of Figure 4). Figure 4 Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) correlates with VLA success rate where VQA scores do not. Across 8 raw vision-language models (VLMs) [59], S2 (left) correlates strongly with SimplerEnv task success after fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs), whereas visual question answering (VQA) scores (right) show virtually no correlation. S2 correlates with WAM success rate more closely than video-quality metrics. We compare S2 with standard video-quality metrics (FID [18], SSIM [52], and PSNR [19]) on 3 of the WAMs, Motus [5], LingBot-VA [28], and Vidar [15], evaluated on RoboTwin. We find that these metrics correlate weakly with task success: SSIM reaches only 𝑟 = +0.558 and PSNR only 𝑟 = +0.468, while FID correlates in the wrong direction, at 𝑟 = +0.680, associating worse video quality with higher success (Figure 5). By contrast, S2 on ALOHA correlates more strongly, at 𝑟 = +0.999. Figure 5 Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) correlates with WAM success rate more closely than video-quality metrics. For 3 world action models (WAMs) evaluated on RoboTwin, video-quality metrics (SSIM, PSNR, FID) show no significant correlations with task success. In contrast, only S2 correctly recovers the success-rate ordering. Only 3 of the 6 WAMs are compared because the others do not generate future video during closed-loop task evaluation. 3.3. S2 Is Robust to Evaluation Choices We next check that the correlation does not depend on particular choice of settings. We test this in two ways. First, we vary how S2 is computed and find that the positive correlation with task success holds. Second, as negative control, we deliberately compute S2 on reference data from mismatched embodiment, where sound metric should lose this correlation. The correlation drops as expected, validating the design of S2. Figure 6 The correlation transfers across reference datasets. For 12 vision-language-action models, Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) on DROID (Franka Panda, left) and BridgeDataV2 (WidowX, right) correlates strongly with the same SimplerEnv-WidowX task success rates. Figure 7 Stable correlations across horizons. For 12 vision-language-action models, Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) and SimplerEnv-WidowX success rate have Pearson 𝑟 > 0.5 at nearly all tested horizons ℎ (future steps) on DROID and BridgeDataV2. S2 is stable across computation choices. In the first check, we vary eight settings: the reference dataset, the trajectory horizon, five implementation choices, and DTW warping. The correlation stays positive under all eight. We discuss the first two below; Appendix C.1 gives per-model S2 by horizon, and Appendices C.2 and C.3 cover the other six. The correlation transfers across reference datasets. We compute S2 on both DROID (Franka Panda) and BridgeDataV2 [49] (WidowX), robots with different arm kinematics, and both correlate near 𝑟 =+0.7 with task success for the 12 VLAs on SimplerEnv (Figure 6). The correlation is also stable across trajectory horizons. It stays above 𝑟 =0.5 at all DROID horizons through ℎ =220 and at BridgeDataV2 horizons from ℎ =3 through 40 (Figure 7). S2 is sensitive to embodiment mismatch. In the negative control, we compute S2 for 3 bimanual WAMs on single-arm reference dataset (DROID) rather than the matched bimanual one (ALOHA). This embodiment mismatch drops the S2success correlation from 𝑟 = +0.999 to 𝑟 = +0.246, indicating that S2 responds to the difference in arm configuration rather than reporting alignment indiscriminately. Appendix C.4 gives the full comparison. 7 4. Representation-Level Explanations with Several phenomena reported for VLAs and WAMs rest only on closed-loop results and still lack representation-level explanation. Because S2 correlates with task success, as shown in Section 3, we use it to explain each of these phenomena, as summarized below: Modality dominance: prior work observes that VLAs often struggle with instruction grounding: they act on what the scene visually suggests rather than on what the language instruction asks [13, 14, 60]. In Section 4.1, we show that after VLA fine-tuning, task success correlates with vision-feature S2 but not text-feature S2, indicating that fine-tuned VLAs draw on what they see, not on the instruction, to produce their motion. Frozen encoders: prior work observes that freezing the vision encoder during VLA finetuning degrades downstream task performance [59]. In Section 4.2, we show that freezing also prevents the S2 gain from end-to-end fine-tuning, indicating that VLAs gain performance by bringing their sensory representation closer to the motor representation. Iterative denoising: prior work observes that WAMs can skip iterative video denoising at test time, decoding actions without generating future video, with little loss in task success [56]. In Section 4.3, we show that the S2 of WAM features is already high at the earliest denoising step and changes little afterwards, indicating that the first denoising steps already yield features aligned closely enough with robot trajectories to act on. Mid-depth blocks: prior work observes that mid-depth blocks of video diffusion transformers matter most for semantic reasoning [51]. In Section 4.4, we show that these blocks also carry the strongest S2, indicating that the layers that reason about video semantics are also the layers most aligned with robot motion. Figure 8 Fine-tuned VLAs rely mainly on visual rather than language representations. We correlate Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) from vision, text, and joint vision-text features (left to right) with SimplerEnv task success rate. Top: For fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs), vision and joint features correlate similarly strongly, while text features correlate weakly. Bottom: For raw vision-language models (VLMs), joint-feature S2 correlates with task success after VLA fine-tuning, while neither modality alone reaches significance. 8 4.1. What Carries the Correlation: Vision, Text, or Both? VLAs often struggle with instruction grounding [13, 14, 60]. We use S2 to explain this at the representation level, asking which modality the correlation with task success depends on: vision, text, or both. In Figure 8, we compute S2 separately for each modality. We take the VLM output tokens read by the action head and form vision features from the image tokens, text features from the instruction tokens, and joint vision-text features from all tokens. Fine-tuned VLAs rely mainly on visual rather than language representations. In the 12 fine-tuned VLAs, S2 from vision features correlates with SimplerEnv success rate at 𝑟 =+0.694, nearly matching the joint vision-text features at 𝑟 =+0.699, whereas text features show no significant correlation at 𝑟 =+0.237. The raw VLMs reverse this pattern: before fine-tuning, text features correlate at 𝑟 =+0.501, more strongly than vision features at 𝑟 =+0.425, and joint vision-text features correlate most strongly at 𝑟 =+0.681. We infer that, after fine-tuning, VLAs produce their motion mainly from visual rather than language representations, which explains their weak instruction grounding. Appendix D.1 reports per-model S2 at all feature positions. 4.2. Freezing Vision Encoders Limits S2 Gain Figure 9 Freezing the vision encoder reduces both Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) and task success rate. For Qwen2.5-VL-3B vision-language-action models fine-tuned on BridgeDataV2, we compare end-to-end training with frozen vision encoder. Freezing lowers S2 from joint vision-text features (top) and SimplerEnv success rate (bottom), linking lower success to weaker alignment. Trajectory horizon ℎ = 7. VLM4VLA [59] reports that VLAs perform substantially worse when their vision encoder stays frozen during fine-tuning. We use S2 to explain this drop at the representation level, testing whether freezing also prevents the sensorimotor-alignment gain from end-to-end fine-tuning. In Figure 9, we compare 2 VLAs that follow the same VLM4VLA [59] recipe and differ only in whether the vision encoder is trained or kept frozen. Freezing the encoder reduces S2 by 41% and SimplerEnv success rate by 40%. These results suggest that end-to-end fine-tuning improves performance by aligning the sensory representation more closely with the motor representation. Appendix D.2 gives the full horizon sweep. 4.3. Features at Early Denoising Steps Already Carry Strong Sensorimotor Alignment Most WAMs generate future video through iterative denoising and decode actions from the resulting latents. Fast-WAM [56] shows that WAMs can skip this video generation and decode actions directly, with little loss in task success. We examine the representation-level reason: whether features at the earliest denoising steps already align with robot trajectories. We measure S2 for 3 WAMs [5, 15, 28] on RoboTwin [33] at 5 positions in each models native denoising schedule, from 0% to 100%, not at matched noise levels (Figure 10a). S2 is already high at the earliest step and remains nearly flat, varying by about 6% at most from its initial value across the 3 models. We infer that early-step features are already sufficiently aligned with robot trajectories to generate actions. Because S2 correlates with WAM success rate (Section 3.1), this result explains why skipping iterative video denoising barely lowers task success. 9 (a) S2 is nearly flat across the schedule. (b) Block 14 has the strongest S2 in all 3 WAMs. Figure 10 Sensorimotor Alignment (S2) is already high at early denoising steps and peaks at mid-depth blocks. For 3 world action models (WAMs), (a) S2 remains nearly flat across denoising, suggesting early-step features already align with robot trajectories; (b) schedule-averaged S2 peaks at Block 14, in the middle of the 30-block backbone. 4.4. Mid-Depth Blocks Carry the Strongest Sensorimotor Alignment Chain-of-Steps [51] shows that mid-depth layers in Video Diffusion Transformers are especially important for semantic reasoning over objects and interactions. We ask whether the layers with the highest S2 also lie in this mid-depth range. In Figure 10b, we compute S2 at different depths of 3 WAMs [5, 15, 28] on RoboTwin. All 3 share 30-block video backbone; we extract features from Blocks 0, 7, 14, 21, and 29. Block 14 yields the highest S2 in every model. This peak falls in the mid-depth range that Chain-of-Steps [51] identifies as semantically important, suggesting that the layers handling video semantic reasoning align most closely with robot motion. Details are in Appendix D.3. 5. Related Work Representation learning in robotics. Many robotics studies pretrain visual representations to improve task performance [32, 34, 40]. However, there remains limited understanding of which representational properties lead to downstream task success. few studies ask what makes pretrained vision encoder useful for robot learning. Hu et al. [20] evaluate 14 frozen vision encoders and find that the correlation between an encoders offline score and downstream task success rate is not stable across policy-learning methods. Burns et al. [8] find that emergent segmentation predicts manipulation success under visual distribution shifts, but only for Vision Transformers. Theia [43] hypothesizes that higher feature-norm entropy improves robot learning, but reports the supporting correlations only within separate groups of encoders. These studies examine only vision encoders rather than broader range of embodied models, and none of them accounts for the trajectories the robot executes when measuring the representation. By contrast, S2 compares 𝑘-nearest-neighbor sets in sensory and motor spaces. The same S2 measure correlates with task success across VLAs, raw VLMs, WAMs, and the encoders that Hu et al. [20] evaluate. Platonic Representation Hypothesis. Recent work has applied the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) [21] to several new domains. In image generation, REPA [54] aligns diffusiontransformer features with self-supervised vision encoders, improving training speed and quality. CREPA [22] extends this recipe to video diffusion. In multimodal understanding, VIRAL [53] re-aligns multimodal large language models (LLMs) with their vision encoders, recovering visual detail lost in multimodal training. For cross-modal alignment, Schnaus et al. [42] match independently trained vision and language encoders through their shared geometry, without paired data. PRH has not yet been brought into robotics; we extend it to robotics by treating 10 robot trajectories as another projection of the world, and find that more capable embodied models align their sensory representations more closely with it. 6. Conclusion We introduce Sensorimotor Alignment (S2), training-free offline metric of alignment between sensory representations and end-effector trajectories. Across VLAs, raw VLMs, and WAMs in simulation, and across real-robot policies, S2 correlates positively with downstream task success, supporting PRH-inspired view of embodiment. S2 correlates more strongly with task success than VQA scores and video-quality metrics, and explains, at the representation level, VLA and WAM phenomena previously observed only through closed-loop results: modality dominance, the performance drop from freezing the vision encoder, the small task-success cost of skipping iterative denoising, and the importance of mid-depth blocks for semantic reasoning. We use S2 only offline as low-cost model-selection and diagnostic tool before closed-loop evaluation, but this correlation motivates optimizing embodied models directly for sensorimotor alignment. Limitations. Our study has three main limitations. (1) The positive relationship between S2 and task success is correlational across the tested models; we have not yet demonstrated that sensorimotor alignment can be used directly during training to improve task success rates. (2) Models with similar S2 values can still achieve different success rates, so S2 is best used as low-cost offline proxy for identifying promising models and VLM backbones before costly fine-tuning or closed-loop testing, which remains the final step of model selection. (3) Our evaluation covers limited model families, benchmarks, and training recipes, few models per comparison, and single real-robot setting; broader generalization remains to be tested.

Sensorimotor Alignment Metric This section gives the full computation of S2 summarized in Section 2: the reference datasets and how we sample from them, the trajectory distance that defines motor neighbors, and the estimator that scores alignment between sensory and motor neighbor sets. A.1. Reference Datasets and Sampling We use three reference datasets: the single-arm DROID and BridgeDataV2 datasets for VLAs, raw VLMs, frozen vision encoders, and real-robot policies, and the bimanual ALOHA dataset for WAMs. DROID and BridgeDataV2 contain teleoperated robot demonstrations with RGB images, proprioceptive states, and language task annotations. Each state is 7D vector = (𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧, 𝜙, 𝜃, 𝜓, 𝑔), where (𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑧) is the end-effector position in meters, (𝜙, 𝜃, 𝜓) are the roll, pitch, and yaw angles in radians, and 𝑔 is the recorded gripper position. This shared format supports the same DTW and S2 computation on both single-arm datasets. BridgeDataV2. BridgeDataV2 [49] contains 53,192 WidowX episodes recorded at 5 Hz. We use the recorded 7D state and retain 38,307 episodes with non-empty task labels. DROID. DROID [26] contains 95,658 episodes on Franka Panda arm recorded at 15 Hz, spanning 86 task categories across 564 scenes in offices, kitchens, and homes. We form the 7D state by concatenating the 6D Cartesian end-effector pose with the gripper position, which is 0 when open and 1 when closed. We retain episodes with language annotation. As the observation image, we use the exterior_image_1_left camera at 180320, the fixed exterior view closest to the third-person camera of BridgeDataV2. ALOHA. For WAMs evaluated on bimanual RoboTwin, we sample 𝑁 = 839 trajectory windows from the bimanual ALOHA dataset [61]. Each trajectory row is the recorded 14dimensional joint-position action vector, with six joints and gripper coordinate per arm. Anchor sampling across horizons.
